1: God tells Moses how to offer a whole animal on the altar: a bull, sheep, goat or bird without blemish, completely burned as a gift to God.
The whole burnt offering stands for giving oneself entirely to God. Christ's sacrifice fulfils it.
2: Rules for offerings of flour, oil and incense, baked or raw. Part is burned and the rest feeds the priests. No yeast, and always salt.
Ordinary food and daily work can be offered to God.
3: An offering in which part is burned, part goes to the priests, and the rest is eaten by the worshipper in a shared meal.
It is a meal of communion with God, a distant figure of the Eucharist.
4: When a priest, the whole people, a leader or an ordinary person sins without meaning to, a set sacrifice is offered and the sin is forgiven.
Sin damages our relationship with God and has to be dealt with, even when it was not deliberate.
5: More cases needing a sacrifice: failing to testify, touching what is unclean, rash oaths. The poor may bring birds or flour instead of a lamb.
God scales what he asks to what a person can afford.
6: Whoever cheats a neighbour must repay in full plus a fifth, then bring an offering. The priests must keep the altar fire burning always.
Being forgiven by God includes making things right with the person wronged.
7: Details for guilt and peace offerings and the priests' share. Eating fat or blood is forbidden.
Worship is ordered by God, not improvised.
8: Moses washes, clothes and anoints Aaron and his sons before the whole community and offers the sacrifices of ordination over seven days.
Priests do not appoint themselves; they are called and consecrated.
9: Aaron offers sacrifice for himself and the people and blesses them. The glory of the Lord appears and fire consumes the offering.
God visibly accepts the worship he himself set up.
10: Two of Aaron's sons offer incense in a way God had not commanded, and fire kills them. God says, "I will be shown holy among those who are near me."
Those who serve at the altar must treat holy things with reverence.
11: Lists of animals Israel may and may not eat. "Be holy, for I am holy."
These rules trained Israel to be distinct. Christ later declared all foods clean.
12: A mother observes a time of purification after giving birth and then brings an offering.
Mary and Joseph kept this law when they presented Jesus in the Temple.
13: Priests examine skin conditions and decide whether a person is clean or must live apart from the camp.
Leprosy becomes a picture of sin, which cuts a person off. Jesus touches and heals lepers.
14: A ritual restores the healed person to the community. Houses with mould are treated in a similar way.
Jesus tells the lepers he heals to show themselves to the priest, as this law required.
15: Rules about ritual uncleanness from bodily discharges and how to be cleansed.
Ritual uncleanness was not sin; it taught reverence for approaching God.
16: Once a year the high priest enters the Holy of Holies with blood for the people's sins. A second goat, the scapegoat, is sent into the desert bearing their guilt.
The Letter to the Hebrews explains that Christ, our high priest, did this once for all with his own blood.
17: Sacrifices may be offered only at the tent of meeting. No one may eat blood, because the life is in the blood and it is given to make atonement.
This prepares for the meaning of Christ's blood poured out for us.
18: God forbids incest, adultery, child sacrifice and other sexual sins practised in Egypt and Canaan.
Israel's family life is to be different from that of the nations around it.
19: A wide set of commands: respect parents, leave part of the harvest for the poor, do not steal, lie or hold grudges, treat the foreigner as a native.
Jesus names verse 18 as the second great commandment.
20: Punishments are set for child sacrifice, consulting the dead, cursing parents and sexual crimes.
God sets his people apart to belong to him.
21: Priests must keep stricter rules about mourning and marriage, because they offer the food of God.
Greater closeness to holy things brings greater responsibility.
22: Priests must be clean to eat the holy food, and animals offered must be without defect.
God deserves the best, not leftovers.
23: The yearly calendar: Sabbath, Passover, Firstfruits, Weeks (Pentecost), Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and Tabernacles.
The Christian year grows from these roots. Easter and Pentecost fulfil Passover and Weeks.
24: The lamp must burn continually and twelve loaves be set before the Lord each Sabbath. A man who curses God's name is punished.
God's name is holy. The bread of the Presence points toward the Eucharist.
25: Every seventh year the land rests. Every fiftieth year slaves go free and land returns to its original family.
The land belongs to God. Jesus announces his mission as a year of the Lord's favour.
26: Obedience will bring rain, harvest, peace and God's presence. Disobedience will bring disease, defeat and exile. Yet God will not forget his covenant.
Even God's punishments aim at bringing his people back.
27: Rules for people, animals, houses and land dedicated to God, and for the tenth of all produce.
A promise made to God must be kept.
